q: Expected inflation falls sharply after a credible long-run policy change, but productive opportunities and saving behavior leave the real rate roughly unchanged. What does the Fisher effect predict?
options: Real interest rates must fall by exactly the same amount as expected inflation.
Nominal rates should stay fixed because only realized inflation affects contracts.
Nominal interest rates should fall as the inflation premium falls.
Nominal interest rates should rise because lower expected inflation raises the inflation premium.

q: A country establishes a credible low-inflation regime. Expected inflation falls from 9 percent to 3 percent, while saving and investment conditions leave the long-run real interest rate near 2 percent. Which outcome best fits the Fisher effect?
options: The nominal interest rate tends to fall from about 11 percent to about 5 percent.
The nominal interest rate tends to rise from about 5 percent to about 11 percent.
The real interest rate must fall from 2 percent to negative 4 percent.
The nominal interest rate should stay near 11 percent because credibility affects only actual inflation.

q: Two long-run episodes have identical expected inflation, but the equilibrium real interest rate is higher in the second because investment demand is stronger. What should happen to the nominal rate?

It must be lower because stronger investment demand reduces nominal rates.

q: An economy enters unexpected deflation while households carry fixed nominal mortgage debt. What happens to the real debt burden, other things equal?

It falls because lower prices make nominal debts shrink automatically.

q: A heavily indebted economy experiences an unexpected 6 percent fall in the overall price level while nominal debts are fixed. Which balance-sheet effect is most likely?
options: Debtors receive an automatic reduction in the nominal face value of their debts.
Creditors lose because every repayment dollar is worth less in real terms.
The fall in the price level is disinflation and therefore cannot affect real debt burdens.

q: Inflation drops from 12 percent to 4 percent after a stabilization program, but the price level continues to rise. A student calls this deflation. What is the best evaluation?

q: The quantity theory predicts that sustained money growth faster than real output growth can raise inflation. In the long-run neutrality framework, what should a student infer about real productive capacity?

Faster money growth must permanently raise productive capacity by the same percentage.
Higher inflation proves output per worker rose by the same amount.
Long-run neutrality requires inflation to be zero whenever money growth exceeds output growth.

q: Refer to the money-market graph. With MD2 and MS2, the equilibrium is point d at r3. If the interest rate is temporarily at point b on MS2 at r4, what adjustment should occur?

Point b is already the equilibrium because it lies on MS2.

Quantity of money demanded exceeds the fixed money supply, so attempts to raise money by selling interest-bearing assets put upward pressure on the interest rate.

q: The central bank increases the money supply and the equilibrium interest rate falls while income and the price level are unchanged. A student says, “Money demand shifted left.” What is the best correction?
options: The fall in the interest rate is a movement along the existing money-demand curve unless a money-demand shifter also changed.
The student is correct because any fall in interest rates shifts the entire money-demand curve left at every quantity, even when income and the price level are unchanged.

Money demand becomes horizontal after an expansionary money-supply change.

q: Refer to the graph. A demand increase has moved the economy to the intersection of AD2 and AS2 at Y2 and P2. If no policy reverses AD2 and long-run adjustment is completed, which comparison between the short-run and long-run effects is supported by the graph?

q: Two economies have identical recessionary gaps. In Economy A, most wages can be reset monthly; in Economy B, most wages are fixed by three-year contracts. With no policy response, which prediction best follows from the long-run adjustment model?

Both economies must return to potential at exactly the same speed because a vertical LRAS fixes the timing as well as the destination.
Neither economy can self-correct without an aggregate-demand policy change because wage and cost adjustment cannot move SRAS.
Economy A should tend to self-correct faster because wages and production costs can adjust sooner.

q: Congress replaces $100 billion of government purchases with a $100 billion tax cut. Households have MPC 0.80. Holding other AD determinants fixed and looking only at the first round, what happens to aggregate demand?

AD rises by $20 billion.
AD rises by $80 billion.
AD falls by $20 billion.

The stimulus becomes contractionary once SRAS begins shifting right.
Self-correction guarantees the stimulus has no effect on aggregate demand.
The delayed stimulus automatically shifts LRAS right by the amount of the original gap.

Lower inflation pressure together with weaker output and higher unemployment.
Lower inflation pressure together with stronger output and lower unemployment.
